title: Edinburgh-rock fiber draw: slice prebuilt vertical cell arrays from preforms
idea: Borrow optical-fiber drawing and seaside rock-candy making: assemble a macroscopic preform of doped-Si-core rods clad in gate glass, metal-glass gate sleeves and capacitor shells, co-draw it ~1000x, bundle and redraw to ~40 nm cell pitch, then wafer-slice the boule crosswise so every slice is a ready-made 4F2 vertical-transistor array needing only top and bottom wiring.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital (fact 4): array pitch is set by draw ratio, not EUV, and one draw-tower run yields thousands of slices; claimed 5-10x lower array capex. Molten-core Si fiber draw exists, but device-grade co-drawn junctions are unproven.

title: Plain-weave bitlines: true and complement swap metal levels every cell
idea: Like warp yarn passing over and under weft, route each bitline pair on two metal levels that cross at every cell pitch through a self-aligned via, so coupling from neighbouring bitlines and wordlines averages out continuously instead of in area-hungry twist regions; open-bitline 4F2 arrays gain folded-array noise immunity.
why: BL-BL coupling eats sense margin in 4F2 open arrays; continuous weaving recovers ~30-50% of signal so Cs can drop from ~5 fF toward ~3 fF (fact 1) or bitlines can double in length, halving sense-amp count (fact 7).

title: Accordion-folded die strip: one thinned strip folded into sixteen tiers
idea: Map-folding origami: fabricate a long strip of 16 array segments on one wafer, thin to ~10 um, replace the silicon between segments with polyimide hinges carrying the bus wiring, then Z-fold the strip into a stack held by die-attach film, so every tier is electrically continuous without TSVs or tier-to-tier alignment.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (fact 6: ~3x wafer area per bit, 20-30% yield loss) and bond-alignment failures; claimed ~2x bits per wafer area versus HBM with stack yield set by per-segment repair.

title: Jelly-roll capacitor: strained bilayer self-rolls into a multi-turn spiral
idea: Borrow battery-cell winding: deposit a flat TiN/high-k/TiN/strained-SiN film beside each access transistor, release a sacrificial underlayer so built-in strain rolls it into a 3-5 turn Swiss roll standing on its anchor, multiplying plate area by the number of turns without any high-aspect-ratio etch.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): area comes from turns, not aspect ratio; three turns of a 300 nm-wide film give ~2-3x the area of a 60:1 pillar per footprint, enabling Cs >10 fF. Rolled MIM tubes exist at micron scale; nanoscale rolling uniformity is the risk.

title: MLCC-style multi-plate lateral capacitor for 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Copy multilayer-ceramic-capacitor construction: inside each tier's lateral capacitor recess, ALD 2N alternating TiN/high-k layers, then open one vertical slit where odd plates are recessed on one side and even plates on the other (like MLCC end terminations), so all plates connect in parallel between storage node and plate line.
why: The lateral capacitor blocks 3D DRAM (fact 2); parallel plates give Cs proportional to plate count instead of recess length, so 4 plate pairs cut lateral cell length ~4x, shrinking cell pitch and lowering the ~26-tier break-even.

title: Lost-wax gyroid: block-copolymer network cast into capacitor electrodes
idea: Investment-casting analogy: fill each capacitor hole with a gyroid-forming block copolymer, remove one block to leave a ~10 nm-strut 3D network (the wax pattern), ALD-coat TiN over it, burn out the polymer, then coat dielectric and top plate, giving a bicontinuous sponge electrode inside the same hole.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 3-5x surface area at equal aspect ratio, so ~5 fF is reachable at AR ~20:1 instead of 60-75:1, relaxing etch and support-lattice steps (fact 4).

title: Slipform tier growth: channels rise through self-aligned tiers
idea: Like slipform concrete poured as the forms climb, grow the vertical channel and the tier stack together: area-selective deposition lays each tier's dielectric and wordline everywhere except on the oxide-semiconductor channel stubs (an inhibitor monolayer binds only there), then selective ALD extends the channels by one tier; no deep hole etch and no per-tier lithography.
why: Eliminates the 60-100:1 vertical etch that caps 3D tier count (fact 2) and removes per-tier masks (fact 4); every tier is self-aligned, so tier count is limited by deposition time rather than etch.

title: Crystal-pulled nanowire forest as 4F2 vertical access transistors
idea: Borrow crystal growth: place SiGe seed nubs at 4F2 sites with spacer-defined dots and grow vertical single-crystal Si nanowires by self-catalysed selective epitaxy, then backfill gate-all-around wordlines and land capacitors on top, so the access transistor is grown rather than etched.
why: 4F2 vertical channels are ~33% smaller than 6F2 (fact 4), and etch-damage-free gate-all-around channels tighten the 13 fA leakage tail that forces refresh (fact 3); self-catalysed growth avoids gold contamination.

title: Honeycomb-core expansion: staggered-anchor films stretch into capacitor walls
idea: Aerospace honeycomb is made by gluing stacked sheets in staggered stripes and pulling them apart; analogously deposit thin metal/dielectric sheets separated by sacrificial layers with staggered anchor stripes, release them, and let programmed stress expand the stack vertically into a hexagonal wall array that becomes shared capacitor plates.
why: Creates tall capacitor walls with no high-AR etch (facts 1, 4), potentially >100:1 effective aspect ratio for the cost of planar deposition; speculative because nanoscale expansion must be uniform across the wafer.

title: Pre-outfitted tier blocks with local sense amps for digital stacking
idea: Shipyards fit pipes and wiring into hull blocks before joining them; likewise give every bonded array tier its own thin-film IGZO sense amplifiers and latches, so inter-tier bonds carry latched digital data at relaxed pitch instead of one analog bitline per bond.
why: Bond pitch can relax ~10x with digital links, raising hybrid-bond yield, and short tier-local bitlines cut CV2 energy; distributes the 49% periphery (fact 7) and trims data-movement energy (fact 5).

title: Duplex-printed pillar: one vertical channel serves front and back cells
idea: Like printing both sides of a sheet, build each vertical pillar with a buried bitline contacting it at mid-height, an upper gate linking it to a front-side capacitor and a lower gate linking it to a backside capacitor formed after bonding and thinning, so one 4F2 footprint stores two bits.
why: Doubles bits per footprint to an effective 2F2 without extra lithographic tiers (fact 4) and halves bitline contacts per bit; risk is two independent gates on one short pillar.

title: Parking-garage helicoid tiers via rotating glancing-angle deposition
idea: Thread-rolling and helical-ramp analogy: deposit the tier stack as one continuous helicoid ramp around a central pillar by glancing-angle deposition while rotating and slowly tilting the wafer, so each tier is one turn of a ramp and all tiers are reachable from the ramp edge without a staircase etch.
why: Staircase area and its many litho-trim loops grow with tier count (facts 2, 4); a helical ramp turns tier access into one contact row. Glancing-angle deposition makes 10-100 nm helices today, but not yet device-grade films.

title: Cotton-candy spun oxide nanofibers as lateral 3D channels
idea: Electrospin aligned In2O3/IGZO precursor nanofibers onto a fast-rotating drum, as in cotton-candy and nonwoven spinning, transfer the aligned mats onto each tier below 400 C and calcine them, giving 10-20 nm lateral channels without epitaxy or Si/SiGe superlattices.
why: The lateral transistor blocks 3D DRAM (fact 2); oxide nanofiber channels with ultralow off-current beat the 13 fA tail and could remove most refresh (fact 3); placement density and alignment are the risk.

title: Car e-coat for capacitors: self-limiting electrophoretic high-k fill
idea: Automotive e-coating paints car bodies conformally because the deposited film insulates and halts further deposition; apply electrophoretic deposition of 3-5 nm SrTiO3/BaTiO3 nanocrystals into high-AR capacitor holes, field-driven and self-limiting, followed by a low-temperature densification anneal.
why: Reaches the k ~70 dielectric that fact 1 says is needed inside AR >100 structures where perovskite ALD struggles, faster and cheaper than ALD cycles; leakage along nanocrystal boundaries is the risk.

title: Running-bond brick stacking: each chiplet straddles two below
idea: Lay DRAM chiplets like bricks in running bond: each upper die is offset by half a die and hybrid-bonded to two lower dies, so vertical links form a 3D mesh with two paths to every die instead of a single TSV column.
why: One bad TSV column kills an HBM stack today (fact 6: 20-30% yield loss); path diversity tolerates failed links and spreads heat; claimed +15-20 points of stack yield.

title: Seeded cast-mono tiers: single-crystal upper layers by rapid melt growth
idea: Solar cast-mono ingots grow single-crystal silicon from seed plates; do the same per tier by depositing amorphous Si/SiGe in oxide crucibles with a seed via to crystalline silicon below, flash-melting for microseconds and letting it recrystallize laterally into single-crystal islands for lateral access transistors.
why: Gives monolithic 3D tiers crystalline channels with a tight leakage tail (fact 3) without strain-limited Si/SiGe superlattice stacks (fact 2); microsecond flash keeps lower tiers below damage temperature.

title: Fermented S-layer protein crystals as sub-10 nm cell masks
idea: Grow bacterial surface-layer (S-layer) proteins by fermentation; they self-crystallize on wafers into 2D lattices of 10-20 nm period, which are metallized or infiltrated into a hard mask that defines vertical-channel or capacitor arrays without EUV.
why: Replaces 5-7 EUV array layers (fact 4) with a bioreactor product costing cents per wafer; defects handled by redundancy mapping; long-range order and registration to periphery are the risk.

title: Balanced-layup tiers: alternating stress plies cancel 3D wafer bow
idea: Composite laminates avoid warp with symmetric, balanced layups; design each 3D DRAM tier pair with opposite-sign film stress (tensile channel ply, compressive wordline ply) and orthogonal line directions, so stress and anisotropy cancel every two tiers instead of accumulating.
why: Wafer bow and overlay distortion cap tier count (fact 2); balanced plies could allow 2-3x more tiers before bow limits, well past the ~26-tier break-even.

title: Tree-ring staircase: CMP a trench-filled stack to expose every tier
idea: Like grinding Damascus steel or turning a log to reveal growth rings, deposit the tier stack conformally into a wide sloped trench and CMP flat, so every tier surfaces as its own band and wordline contacts land with one lithography step instead of 10-30 resist-trim and etch cycles.
why: Staircase formation costs area and many litho/etch loops as tiers grow (facts 2, 4); one CMP plus one contact mask could cut staircase cost >5x and area ~2x.

title: Mortise-and-tenon bond pads enable per-cell split-wafer DRAM
idea: Joinery self-aligns parts; etch conical tenons on a transistor wafer and matching mortises on a separate capacitor wafer so mechanical engagement during hybrid bonding pulls overlay from ~100 nm to ~10 nm, allowing one bond per cell at ~200 nm pitch, with transistors from logic-like lines and deep capacitors from MEMS-like lines.
why: Splits the cell's two incompatible processes (capacitor thermal budget vs transistor leakage, facts 1 and 3) onto optimized wafers; per-cell bonding is ~10x too coarse today, and self-alignment is the enabler.

title: Roll-to-roll memory book: one hundred laminated oxide-TFT foils
idea: Print-shop analogy: produce oxide-TFT gain-cell arrays roll-to-roll on 5 um polyimide or steel foil, cut sheets, and laminate 100 of them into a book whose spine is edge-bonded with anisotropic conductive film to a CMOS controller.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4) and U.S. manufacturability: R2R lines cost ~1% of a DRAM fab; bits per sheet are low, but 100 penny sheets could give a ~$1-2/GB capacity tier; access may sit at 100 ns-1 us rather than 10-100 ns.

title: Co-fired tiers: deposit all oxide channels amorphous, activate once
idea: Like co-firing green ceramic tapes in one kiln pass, deposit every tier's oxide-semiconductor channel and high-k amorphous at room temperature, then run one final anneal for the whole stack instead of annealing each tier and re-baking the lower tiers N times.
why: Accumulated thermal budget drifts lower-tier threshold voltage and leakage (facts 2, 3); one co-fire makes tier N match tier 1 and removes N-1 anneals (~20-30% cycle time).

title: Roll-formed corrugated tiers: long-channel lateral transistors in short pitch
idea: Roll-formed corrugated sheet gets length without footprint; deposit each tier over a pre-patterned sinusoidal base so the lateral access transistor's channel follows the wave, giving ~2x channel length (and extra flank width) inside the same cell pitch.
why: A longer effective channel suppresses short-channel leakage and the refresh-forcing tail (fact 3) by up to ~10x while keeping 3D cell pitch, making lateral transistors viable (fact 2).

title: Puff-pastry lamination: binary-tree bonding of mature-node DRAM wafers
idea: Laminated dough multiplies layers by folding; hybrid-bond pairs of thinned 2x-nm DRAM wafers face to face, then bond pairs of pairs, so a 16-tier stack needs only 4 serial bond-and-thin steps run in parallel on existing bonding and grinding tools, with relaxed 10 um edge TSVs.
why: 16x bits per footprint with zero new lithography (fact 4), using fully depreciated 2x-nm DRAM fabs and OSAT tools; serial cycle time scales as log2(N) and every tier is pre-tested.

title: Newspaper-press memory: IGZO DRAM arrays in idle LCD panel fabs
idea: Like a newspaper press trading resolution for acreage, run 2T0C/1T1C IGZO arrays at ~1 um rules on Gen-6/8.5 glass in under-used LCD and LTPS fabs, dice them into memory tiles and pair them with small CMOS controller chiplets as a CXL capacity tier.
why: At ~4 um2/bit a Gen-8.5 panel holds ~170 GB per layer; at ~$500-1000 per processed panel that is ~$3-6/GB with no new fab; IGZO's low leakage eases refresh, but access will be ~100 ns-class.

title: Roof-shingle HBM: offset die stacks with 3D-printed edge traces
idea: Stack legacy DDR4/LPDDR dies offset like roof shingles so each die's edge pad row is exposed, then aerosol-jet 3D-print 20 um-pitch copper traces down the staircase to a logic base die, giving a wide bus without TSVs.
why: Removes TSV area and yield tax (fact 6) with installed OSAT tools; ~1-2k traces per edge gives HBM2-class bandwidth from mature dies.

title: Cross-grain veneer slicing: epitaxial superlattice edges define sub-10 nm lines
idea: Plywood shows its plies when cut across the grain; grow a 400-layer Si/SiGe superlattice in a trailing-fab epi reactor, cleave and polish its edge, recess the SiGe, and use the edge as a stamp (superlattice nanowire pattern transfer) to print 8-10 nm half-pitch metal line arrays onto array wafers.
why: Line pitch is set by angstrom-level epitaxial thickness control instead of EUV (fact 4), giving wordline/bitline grids for 4F2 cross-point arrays on 90-28 nm tooling.

title: Ball-bearing packing: colloidal monolayer masks for hex vertical-channel arrays
idea: Like ball bearings settling in a tray, float a Langmuir monolayer of 40-60 nm silica spheres onto wafers, shrink them in plasma to set hole size, and etch a hexagonal vertical-channel array with mature etch tools; periphery uses ordinary litho and colloid grain boundaries are mapped out as spare rows.
why: Dense hex arrays at ~50 nm pitch without immersion or EUV (fact 4); at roughly a quarter of leading-edge wafer cost, cost per bit approaches mainstream for capacity memory.

title: Anodized-cookware pores: AAO capacitor forests on 28 nm logic
idea: Anodize a thick aluminium BEOL layer on 28-40 nm logic wafers to self-organize 60-80 nm-pitch pores with AR >100:1, ALD TiN/high-k/TiN into them, and tie each pore cluster to a logic-node access transistor to make stand-alone 1T1C DRAM in foundries that never made DRAM.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): AAO reaches AR 100+ by electrochemistry, not etch, for Cs >10 fF per cell, and it enlists U.S. trailing logic fabs with only a plating-bath module added.

title: Wire-bonder pin forest: bond-via arrays link legacy dies to logic
idea: Use installed wire bonders as 3D printers to stand dense forests of vertical 25 um copper wires on a logic die, mold and grind them flat, and face-down-bond mature DRAM dies on top as an HBM-like wide bus with no TSV process.
why: Sidesteps the HBM TSV tax (fact 6) entirely in existing OSAT lines (~10-20k wires per stack) and places memory adjacent to compute to cut I/O energy toward ~2 pJ/bit (fact 5).

title: Nano-velcro reworkable stacking: unhook and replace bad tiers
idea: Template-electroplate copper nanowire hook fields on stack pads in existing bump lines so mating fields interlock at room temperature like Velcro; test the stack, peel off any bad die, press in a good one, then anneal to make the joints permanent.
why: Turns the 20-30% HBM stack yield loss (fact 6) into a repairable step, so stack yield approaches die yield, with no bonding thermal budget.

title: Baker's dozen tier: build N+1 legacy dies, cull the weakest
idea: Bakers add a thirteenth roll against shortfalls; stack 9 mature DRAM dies for an 8-high product and route them through a small switch matrix in the base die so the worst tier, by retention or row-hammer threshold, is disabled after assembly test.
why: Converts stack failures into a ~12% silicon spare and lets marginal binned-out mature dies ship, lifting usable stack supply ~15-25% (facts 6, 9).

title: Marquetry slab: reconstituted wafer of harvested partial-good banks
idea: Like inlaid marquetry made from offcuts, dice partially failing mature DRAM dies along bank boundaries, inlay the good banks into a pocketed reconstituted wafer on existing fan-out lines, and wire them with one coarse RDL into a wafer-scale memory slab with a routing table.
why: Recovers bits from scrapped dies (~5-15% of output) and builds large capacity slabs with no new fab, lowering scarce-resource use per usable bit.

title: Coin-sorter assembly: fluidic self-assembly of DRAM micro-chiplets onto logic
idea: Like coin sorters dropping coins into shaped slots, agitate 300 um shape-keyed mature-node DRAM micro-chiplets in fluid over a logic wafer with matching receptor wells so they fall in and lock, then planarize and connect them with one RDL, placing thousands per minute.
why: Puts memory directly over compute using cheap mature dies, cutting data-movement energy (fact 5) and pick-and-place capex; fluidic self-assembly is proven for RFID and microLED.

title: Half-tone staircase: grayscale mask forms all tier steps at once
idea: Half-tone printing renders gray by dot density; use a sub-resolution dot grayscale reticle on an i-line/KrF stepper to form a stepped resist profile, then a proportional etch transfers all N staircase steps for a 3D array in one litho+etch instead of N trim-etch cycles.
why: Staircase cost and time scale with tier count (fact 2); one exposure on a depreciated scanner cuts staircase loops >10x for 32-64 tiers.

title: Veneer-peel tiers: spall device layers instead of grinding wafers away
idea: Veneer mills peel thin sheets from a log instead of sawing it; after front-end processing on mature lines, deposit a stressed nickel layer and controlled-spall the top 10-20 um device layer for stacking, then repolish and reuse the parent substrate 5-10 times.
why: Backgrinding for stacking discards ~97% of each wafer; spalling cuts wafer and Spruce Pine crucible consumption per stacked tier ~5x and makes thin tiers with only a spall station added.

title: Arsenal conversion: retool legacy 3D-NAND lines for vertical oxide DRAM
idea: Like WWII car plants converted to bombers, fund conversion of 48-96-layer 3D NAND lines, which need no EUV and already own deep-hole etch and staircase tools, to make vertical-string oxide-channel gain-cell DRAM under a Defense Production Act Title III style program with offtake guarantees.
why: Fastest route to 3D DRAM tiers (fact 2) without a $15B, 3-5 year fab; reuses depreciated deep-etch capacity and policy can unlock it in months.

title: Chassis-body marriage: trailing U.S. logic fabs supply DRAM periphery wafers
idea: Automakers build chassis and bodies on separate lines and marry them; DRAM makers would fabricate array-only wafers and buy periphery wafers (sense amps, decoders, I/O) from U.S. 28-65 nm foundries under contract, then hybrid-bond the two.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7); offloading it frees ~40% of DRAM-fab wafer starts for arrays and creates U.S. content as a periphery-as-a-service business.

title: Photographic contact print: Talbot self-imaging for periodic cell arrays
idea: Use displacement Talbot lithography, a contact-print-like method exploiting self-imaging of periodic masks, to expose dense hexagonal capacitor or channel arrays below 100 nm pitch with mature UV sources, then spacer pitch-split to ~40 nm.
why: Array layers are perfectly periodic, exactly Talbot's sweet spot; replaces immersion/EUV array exposures (fact 4) with ~$1-3M tools.

title: Vinyl-record pressing: nanoimprint stampers for capacitor and channel layers
idea: Records are pressed from nickel stampers replicated from one master; write one e-beam master of the capacitor-hole layer, electroform daughter stampers, and imprint every wafer in mature fabs, aligning to coarse periphery marks.
why: Swaps EUV exposures (fact 4) for imprint at a fraction of tool cost; imprint defects are tolerable in regular arrays with row redundancy.

title: Electroforming bath: superconformal cobalt fill replaces CVD tungsten wordlines
idea: Jewelry electroforming fills molds bottom-up; use suppressor/accelerator plating chemistry for bottom-up cobalt or copper fill of buried wordlines and 3D lateral wordline recesses on existing plating tools, dropping CVD tungsten.
why: Removes a ~80% China-sourced tungsten dependency and lowers wordline resistance ~2-3x, allowing longer wordlines and fewer drivers (fact 7).

title: Crepe-paper electrodes: controlled buckling doubles capacitor area
idea: Like crepe paper or pleated filters gaining area through wrinkles, deposit the bottom electrode on a compliant sacrificial underlayer with compressive mismatch so it buckles into 20-40 nm-wavelength wrinkles before dielectric and top-electrode ALD on mature tools.
why: +1.5-2x area per footprint permits lower aspect ratio or trailing-node cells (fact 1) without new high-AR etchers.

title: Post-tensioned tendons: one through-stack via fill for N tiers
idea: Precast bridge segments are stacked with aligned ducts and one tendon is threaded through; stack thinned tier wafers with pre-opened, tapered, aligned ducts made by relaxed trailing litho, then one electroplating step fills a continuous via through every tier.
why: Replaces N separate TSV reveal-and-fill sequences with one, cutting HBM TSV cost and yield loss (fact 6); tapered ducts tolerate misalignment.

title: Tailor's marker nesting: shape dies to harvest wafer-edge silicon
idea: Garment cutters nest pattern pieces to minimize scrap; design mature-node memory as small self-contained hexagonal banks that plasma dicing can cut in any outline, so partial wafer-edge regions yield sellable small dies.
why: Recovers ~5-10% more bits per wafer from existing capacity with zero new fab, raising usable supply.

title: Oil-well drilling: revive U.S. deep-trench eDRAM modules as DRAM bricks
idea: Deep-trench capacitors are drilled into the substrate like oil wells; restart deep-trench eDRAM process modules in U.S. SOI trailing fabs to make stand-alone eDRAM brick chiplets with trench Cs above 10 fF for L4 and near-memory caches.
why: Proven 1T1C trench cells with long retention at 22-32 nm, no EUV, U.S.-made; displaces part of HBM demand for cache-like working sets.

title: Resin-vat recoating: spin-on liquid oxide tiers cured by UV
idea: SLA 3D printers recoat liquid resin and cure layer by layer; stack tiers by spin-coating solution In-Zn-O semiconductor and spin-on high-k, curing each with deep-UV photochemical activation below 250 C on existing coat/track tools, patterned with KrF masks.
why: Vacuum-free tier deposition slashes per-tier capex and lets old track tools add oxide gain-cell tiers on logic BEOL (facts 2, 4), avoiding new ALD and sputter capacity.
